content_voiceover: This question tests understanding of primary myelofibrosis pathophysiology by asking which statement is not true. Option A is correct, median age at diagnosis is 65 to 70 years, though rare pediatric and even neonatal cases occur. Option B is correct, case reports of myelofibrosis in lupus patients support an immune mediated mechanism of marrow connective tissue hyperplasia in some cases. Option C is the false statement, and this is the one to focus on for boards. It claims that neoplastic myeloproliferation dominates in the erythroid and megakaryocytic lineages, producing an intensely cellular marrow with only mild granulocytosis and thrombocytosis. That is backwards from the true biology. In primary myelofibrosis, the dominant proliferating lineages are megakaryocytic and granulocytic, while erythropoiesis is typically reduced, contributing to anemia. And critically, as the disease progresses, the marrow becomes progressively fibrotic and hypocellular, not intensely cellular. Option D is correct, massive increases in splenoportal blood flow from extramedullary hematopoiesis, combined with decreased hepatic vascular compliance or hepatic vein thrombosis, can produce severe portal hypertension and ascites. Option E is correct, extramedullary hematopoietic foci on serosal surfaces can cause pleural, pericardial, or abdominal effusions, sometimes massive.
keypoints: Megakaryocytic and granulocytic lineages proliferate in PMF, while erythropoiesis is typically reduced
Progressive PMF marrow becomes fibrotic and hypocellular, not intensely cellular as option C claims
Median age at diagnosis is 65 to 70, but pediatric and neonatal cases are reported
Splenoportal hyperperfusion plus reduced hepatic vascular compliance can cause severe portal hypertension
Extramedullary hematopoiesis on serosal surfaces can cause massive pleural or pericardial effusions
keypoint_voiceover: Remember the biology backwards from option C, PMF is driven by megakaryocytic and granulocytic proliferation with reduced erythropoiesis, and the marrow trends toward fibrosis and hypocellularity over time rather than staying intensely cellular.
